---
description: Be asked about your business properly, and get a written brief before anything is built

The builder wants to talk about: **(whatever the builder typed after the command name)**

If that is empty, ask them what they have in mind and wait. One question, no menu.

## What this phase produces

One document — `prd.md`, the brief — written in the builder's own words: what the
software is for, who uses it, what it must do, what it must never do, and how
they will know it works. `/describe` turns that brief into the spec.

Nothing is built here. No code, no project, no files outside the brief.

**This step is optional, and sometimes it should be skipped.** If what they want
is small and they have already said it clearly — "a contact form on my website
that emails me" — say so and point them at `/describe`. Twenty questions about a
contact form teaches them that this framework wastes their time, and they will
stop answering carefully on the day it matters.

## Read first

- `.edgepoint/protocol/decisions.md` — which questions are yours and which are theirs
- `.edgepoint/protocol/questions.md` — the shape of a question; it is not optional
- `.edgepoint/protocol/escalation.md` — so you recognise an edge while they are still talking
- `.edgepoint/recipes/README.md`, and every recipe that plausibly covers this —
  each one lists the business questions it genuinely raises. **Those are your
  questions.** If a recipe lists three, you ask at most three.
- `.edgepoint/standard/` — so you never ask about something already settled

## How the interview goes

One question at a time. Wait for the answer. Absorb it before asking the next —
a question that ignores what they just said tells them you are working from a
list, and people stop thinking when they are being processed.

Their vocabulary throughout. If they say *enquiry*, everything you write says
enquiry. If they say *guests* rather than *customers*, so do you. The brief is
worth reading only if it sounds like their business.

Every so often — three or four questions in — play back what you have so far in
two or three sentences and ask whether you have it right. That is where the
misunderstandings surface, and it costs one exchange to fix something that
otherwise gets built.

## The ground to cover

An agenda, not a questionnaire. Skip anything they have already answered, and
follow what they tell you rather than the order below when their answer opens
something up.

1. **Today, without the software.** What happens now, who does it, where it goes
   wrong, how often. Start here always: it is the only part that needs no
   imagination from them, and it is where the real requirements are.
2. **Who touches it.** Every kind of person, in their words — customers, the
   receptionist, the branch manager. What each one must be able to do, and what
   each one must never be able to see or do. Vagueness here becomes a security
   hole later.
3. **What people need to do.** The handful of things, most important first. Plain
   verbs: book an appointment, cancel it, see tomorrow's list.
4. **The rules that would still be true on paper.** No double bookings. Refunds
   within 14 days. A customer never sees another customer's details. These are
   the business's rules, not the software's.
5. **Money, if any moves.** What is charged, who pays whom, when, what happens if
   a payment fails, whether anything is refunded. Prices in pesos, hosted
   checkout and what it accepts are settled — do not raise any of that.
6. **What is kept about people.** What personal information they need, why, and
   for how long. Listen here for the edges in `protocol/escalation.md` — health
   information, government ID numbers, anything about children — because they
   arrive sounding like ordinary requests.
7. **This version, and not this version.** What is in the first thing they get,
   and what is deliberately left out. The cheapest question in the interview:
   anything unstated, they will assume is included.
8. **What "it works" looks like.** What they would sit down and try, on the day
   it is delivered, to satisfy themselves it does what they asked.

## When to stop

**Stop when you could write every section of the brief without guessing.** That
is usually somewhere between eight and fifteen questions. It is never forty.

Stop sooner when any of these happen:

- Their answers stop changing the picture — you are collecting detail, not
  requirements.
- They say "whatever you think" twice in a row. Take your recommendation, note it
  as chosen by default, move on. More information will not produce an opinion
  they do not have.
- They want to stop. Then stop. Write the brief with what you have and mark what
  is missing — a half-answered brief still beats none, and `/clarify` picks up
  the rest.

## Decide, don't ask

Everything technical is already settled and asking about it is the one failure
this framework exists to prevent. Resolve it from `standard/` and the recipes,
and write what you resolved into the brief's *Settled without asking* section.

That section is not decoration. It is what stops `/clarify` putting the same
question to them a second time, and it is the record a developer reads later.

If they push a technical decision at you — "should this be an app or a website?"
— answer briefly, say it is already settled, and return to their side of it.

## At the edge

If something they describe sits outside the Standard, do not stall the interview
over it and do not promise it. Keep going, and at the end tell them plainly: what
you can build, what needs a developer, why, and what you would do instead today.
`protocol/escalation.md` has the shape and the wording.

Write it into the brief under *Needs a developer*. It becomes `escalations.md`
when the spec exists.

## Writing the brief

Only when the interview is over:

1. Run `edgepoint new "<what they call this>"`. It creates `specs/NNN-slug/` and
   prints the path. Doing it now rather than at the start means an interview they
   abandoned halfway leaves nothing behind.
2. Write `prd.md` in that folder, to the shape below.
3. Leave every other file in that folder alone. `spec.md`, `plan.md` and
   `tasks.md` belong to `/describe` and `/clarify` — writing them here produces
   two documents that disagree.

Rules for the prose:

- **No technology in it.** Same rule as `spec.md`: if a product name appears, it
  is in the wrong document. "Customers pay with GCash" is their business and
  belongs; naming what processes the payment does not.
- **Every statement is theirs or marked as yours.** Anything you decided by
  default says so, in the line where it appears.
- **Acceptance criteria are things they could try**, written as sentences they
  would recognise — not "the handler validates the payload".
- **Don't pad.** A brief for a small thing is one page. Length here is not
  thoroughness; it is a document nobody reads.

### The shape

```markdown
# <what they call it>

*From an interview on <date>, written in the builder's own words. This is the
brief the spec gets written from — if anything here is wrong, now is the cheap
time to say so.*

## What this is for
<!-- Two or three sentences: what they want, and why it matters to their
business. How it works today, and what is wrong with today. -->

## Who uses it
<!-- Each kind of person, in their words. What they can do, and what they must
never be able to do. -->

## What people need to do
<!-- The things a person can do, most important first. Plain verbs. -->

## What it will not do
<!-- Deliberately out of this version. -->

## Rules the business cares about
<!-- The constraints that would still be true if the software didn't exist. -->

## Money
<!-- What is charged, who pays, when, what happens when a payment fails, what is
refundable. Omit this section entirely if no money moves. -->

## Information about people
<!-- What is kept about identifiable people, why, and for how long. Omit only if
genuinely nothing is. -->

## How we'll know it works
<!-- Acceptance criteria, in their sentences. These become the tests. -->

- When I ..., then ...
- When I ..., then ...

## Settled without asking
<!-- Technical decisions you made for them and the rule you made them from. One
line each. This is what stops /clarify asking them the same things. -->

- <decision> — <rule or recipe it came from>

## Needs a developer
<!-- Anything outside the Standard, what you'd build instead, and what it would
take. Omit the section if there is nothing. -->

## Still open
<!-- Business questions the interview didn't settle. /clarify picks these up, so
an honest list here is worth more than a tidy one. -->
```

## Then tell them

A short paragraph, not a document dump: what you understood they want, what you
decided on their behalf, anything that needs a developer, and what is still open.

Tell them where the brief is and that it is worth ten minutes of their time —
being wrong on paper costs nothing, and being wrong after `/build` costs a
rebuild. Then point them at `/describe`, which writes the spec from it without
asking them to say any of this again.
